idiom_name: closure implementing Fn/FnMut/FnOnce; Waker for async runtimes
implementation_notes: A Rust callback is a closure, and the three closure traits encode the invocation contract: Fn for callables that can run repeatedly and concurrently, FnMut for callbacks that mutate captured state, and FnOnce for the single-shot completion callback. A generic parameter (impl Fn(&T)) is the zero-cost form; Box<dyn Fn>, Arc<dyn Fn> or a struct field store the callback when the type cannot be generic, and an Option<Box<dyn FnOnce>> taken with Option::take() is the standard way to store a one-shot completion without risking a double call. For asynchronous work the runtime's callback is std::task::Waker rather than a user function: futures are driven by wakers and executors, and channels or async/await replace stored completion callbacks. The classic trait-object form is still right when the callback contract needs several methods or a named, object-safe API.
pitfalls: A stored closure that borrows caller state cannot outlive the call: the compiler forces the choice between moving owned state in, naming a lifetime, or requiring 'static (which is why callbacks in long-lived registries are usually Arc'd).
Calling an FnOnce kept in shared state needs interior mutability plus Option::take(); invoking it twice is impossible by construction but a panicking unwrap on the taken slot is the usual failure.
Re-entrant callbacks that mutably borrow the same RefCell panic at run time, and a Mutex held across the callback deadlocks - the borrow checker cannot see through the callback boundary.
Dropping the handler (or the future that holds a Waker) silently cancels the notification, so the completion is never delivered and the caller appears to hang.
